nameStory: This tiger beetle earned its 'claybank' name from its love of steep clay banks and exposed clay soil where it hunts for prey. The 'tiger' part comes from these beetles' fierce predatory nature and lightning-fast speed as they chase down other insects, much like their big cat namesake stalking prey.
description: The Common Claybank Tiger Beetle is a colorful, fast-moving predator about half an inch long. Its metallic back shimmers with reddish-purple hues, though some individuals appear dull green or brown instead. These speedy hunters have large, bulging eyes and powerful jaws for catching other insects. With their iridescent sheen and quick movements, they're like tiny jeweled race cars of the insect world.

idTips.label: Clay Bank Habitat
idTips.description: Look for them exclusively on steep, bare clay banks that feel moist and sticky to the touch, especially along eroded hillsides and stream cuts

idTips.label: Reddish-Purple Sheen
idTips.description: The back has a metallic reddish-purple shimmer that catches sunlight like polished copper, though some appear dull green or brown

idTips.label: Lightning Speed
idTips.description: They dart away incredibly fast when approached, often running in short bursts before stopping abruptly to assess threats

idTips.label: Size and Build
idTips.description: About 12-16mm long (roughly half an inch) with a robust, sturdy body that feels solid if gently handled

idTips.label: Large Eyes
idTips.description: Prominent, bulging compound eyes that give them excellent vision for spotting both prey and predators

habitat: Common Claybank Tiger Beetles are specialists of steep, moist clay banks and exposed clay soils throughout New England. You'll find them along eroded hillsides, stream cuts, construction sites, and roadside embankments where bare clay is exposed to sunlight. They prefer areas where the clay stays somewhat moist but isn't waterlogged, often on south-facing slopes that get good sun exposure.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge and become active as temperatures warm, often seen sunning themselves on clay banks during mild afternoons.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most visible hunting during warm, sunny days. They're most active in mid-morning and late afternoon.
seasonality.fall: Adults remain active into early fall, though they become less active as temperatures cool and may seek shelter in clay crevices.
seasonality.winter: Adults overwinter buried in clay soil or hidden in cracks, completely inactive until spring temperatures return.

funFact: These beetles can live for up to 3 years as adults, which is remarkably long for an insect - most beetles live only a few months! During this time, they may experience six or more New England winters, making them some of the most weather-hardened insects in our region.
confusionNotes: Other tiger beetles in New England prefer sandy areas, so if you're seeing a metallic beetle on clay soil, it's almost certainly this species. The clay habitat is your best identification clue - remember 'claybank beetle loves clay banks!'
contextualKnowledge: Despite their fearsome name and predatory nature, tiger beetles are actually beneficial insects that help control pest populations. They're considered indicator species for healthy ecosystems, so finding them suggests the local environment is in good condition.
compareHints: Unlike the Six-spotted Tiger Beetle which prefers woodland paths, or the Bronzed Tiger Beetle found on sandy beaches, the Common Claybank Tiger Beetle is the only New England tiger beetle that specializes in clay habitats. While other tiger beetles may occasionally visit clay areas, this species is the clay specialist with its distinctive reddish-purple coloration.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's tiger beetles, the six-spotted stands out for its pure metallic green color - the bronzed tiger beetle has more copper tones, while the festive tiger beetle is darker with different spot patterns.

Among New England's tiger beetles, the Bronzed Tiger Beetle is distinguished by its warm copper-bronze coloration, while the Six-spotted Tiger Beetle shines bright metallic green and the Purple Tiger Beetle displays cooler purple-blue tones.
Among New England's tiger beetles, the festive tiger beetle is distinguished by its particular pattern of white markings and metallic coloration.
Among New England's tiger beetles, the Hairy-necked is the only one with those distinctive fuzzy neck hairs.
Among New England's tiger beetles, the twelve-spotted is unique for having exactly twelve spots on a dark body.
Among New England's tiger beetles, the Oblique-lined stands out with its exceptionally large compound eyes and distinctive diagonal white markings.
Among New England's tiger beetles, the Big Sand Tiger Beetle stands out for its robust, chunky build compared to the more slender Six-spotted or Bronzed Tiger Beetles.
Unlike the bright metallic green Six-spotted Tiger Beetle with its obvious white spots, the Purple Tiger Beetle shows deep purple metallic colors without distinct white markings.
